mn125:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
mn125:2.1: Now on that occasion the novice Aciravata was living in a forest hut.
mn125:2.2: Then Prince Jayasena, while wandering and walking for exercise, went to the novice Aciravata and exchanged greetings with him.
mn125:2.3: When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he sat down at one side. When he had done so, Prince Jayasena said to the novice Aciravata:
mn125:2.5: “A bhikkhu who lives here diligent, ardent, and self-controlled might achieve unification of mind.”’
mn125:2.6: ‘That is so, Prince, that is so.
mn125:2.7: A bhikkhu who lives here diligent, ardent, and self-controlled might achieve unification of mind.’
mn125:3.1: ‘It would be good if Master Aggivessana taught me the Dhamma according as he has heard and mastered it.’
mn125:3.2: ‘I cannot teach you the Dhamma, Prince, according as I have heard and mastered it.
mn125:3.3: For, Prince, were I to teach you the Dhamma according as I have heard and mastered it, and you did not know the meaning of what I said, that would be wearisome and a bother for me.’
mn125:4.1: ‘Let Master Aggivessana teach me the Dhamma according as he has heard and mastered it.
mn125:4.2: Perhaps I might know the meaning of what Master Aggivessana said.’
mn125:4.3: ‘I might teach you the Dhamma, Prince, according as I have heard and mastered it.
mn125:4.4: If you know the meaning of what I say, that will be good;
mn125:4.5: if you do not know the meaning of what I say, then leave it at that and question me no further about it.’
mn125:4.6: ‘Let Master Aggivessana teach me the Dhamma according as he has heard and mastered it.
mn125:4.7: If I know the meaning of what Master Aggivessana said, that will be good;
mn125:4.8: if I do not know the meaning of what Master Aggivessana said, then I shall leave it at that, and question Master Aggivessana no further about it.’
mn125:5.1: Then the novice Aciravata taught Prince Jayasena the Dhamma according as he had heard and mastered it.
mn125:5.2: When this was said, Prince Jayasena said to the novice Aciravata:
mn125:5.3: ‘It is impossible, Master Aggivessana, it cannot be, that a bhikkhu who lives diligent, ardent, and self-controlled might achieve unification of mind.’
mn125:5.4: Then, having told the novice Aciravata that it was impossible and could not be, Prince Jayasena got up from his seat and departed.
mn125:6.1: Then, soon after Prince Jayasena had gone, the novice Aciravata went to the Blessed One, and after paying homage to him, he sat down at one side.
mn125:6.2: When he had done so, the novice Aciravata recounted to the Blessed One all his conversation with Prince Jayasena.
mn125:7.1: When this was said, the Blessed One said to the novice Aciravata:
mn125:7.3: That what is to be known through renunciation, seen through renunciation, reached through renunciation, realized through renunciation, should ever be known, seen, reached, or realized by Prince Jayasena, who lives in the midst of sensual desires, enjoys sensual desires, is devoured by thoughts of sensual desires, is consumed by the fever of sensual desires, and is bent on seeking sensual desires—that is not possible.
mn125:8.1: ‘Suppose, Aggivessana, there were two tamable elephants, or two tamable horses, or two tamable oxen, that were well-tamed and well-disciplined, and also two tamable elephants or two tamable horses or two tamable oxen that were untamed and undisciplined.
mn125:8.3: those two tamable elephants, horses, or oxen that were well-tamed and well-disciplined—being tamed, would they go as the tamed go, would they reach the grade of the tamed?’
mn125:8.5: ‘But those two tamable elephants, horses, or oxen that were untamed and undisciplined—being untamed, would they go as the tamed go, would they reach the grade of the tamed, as those two well-tamed, well-disciplined elephants, horses, or oxen did?’
mn125:8.7: ‘So too, Aggivessana, that what is to be known through renunciation, seen through renunciation, reached through renunciation, realized through renunciation, should ever be known, seen, reached, or realized by Prince Jayasena, who lives in the midst of sensual desires, enjoys sensual desires, is devoured by thoughts of sensual desires, is consumed by the fever of sensual desires, and is bent on seeking sensual desires—that is not possible.
mn125:9.1: ‘Suppose, Aggivessana, there were a high rock not far from a village or town.
mn125:9.2: Then two friends went out from that village or town and approached that rock hand in hand; having approached, one friend remained below at the foot of the rock while the other climbed up on the rock.
mn125:9.3: Then the friend standing below at the foot of the rock said to the friend standing on top of the rock:
mn125:9.4: “Well, friend, what do you see, standing on top of the rock?”
mn125:9.6: “Standing on top of the rock, friend, I see beautiful parks, beautiful woods, beautiful meadows, and beautiful lakes.”
mn125:9.8: “It is impossible, friend, it cannot be, that you, standing on top of the rock, should see beautiful parks, beautiful woods, beautiful meadows, and beautiful lakes.”
mn125:9.9: Then the friend standing on top of the rock came down to the foot of the rock, and taking that friend by the arm, made him climb to the top of the rock, and then, after letting him breathe a little, said:
mn125:9.10: “Well, friend, what do you see, standing on top of the rock?”
mn125:9.12: “Standing on top of the rock, friend, I see beautiful parks, beautiful woods, beautiful meadows, and beautiful lakes.”
mn125:9.14: “Just a little earlier, friend, you spoke thus—we heard you say this:
mn125:9.15: ‘It is impossible, friend, it cannot be, that you, standing on top of the rock, should see beautiful parks, beautiful woods, beautiful meadows, and beautiful lakes.’
mn125:9.16: But just now you spoke thus—we heard you say this:
mn125:9.17: ‘Standing on top of the rock, friend, I see beautiful parks, beautiful woods, beautiful meadows, and beautiful lakes.’”
mn125:9.19: “That is because, friend, I was obstructed by this great rock, so that I did not see what was there to be seen.”
mn125:10.1: ‘By something greater than that, Aggivessana, Prince Jayasena is obstructed, screened, blocked, and shut off by the mass of ignorance.
mn125:10.2: So too, that what is to be known through renunciation, seen through renunciation, reached through renunciation, realized through renunciation, should ever be known, seen, reached, or realized by Prince Jayasena, who lives in the midst of sensual desires, enjoys sensual desires, is devoured by thoughts of sensual desires, is consumed by the fever of sensual desires, and is bent on seeking sensual desires—that is not possible.
mn125:11.1: ‘If, Aggivessana, these two similes had occurred to you in regard to Prince Jayasena, he would, without wonder, have acquired confidence in you, and having acquired confidence he would have shown you the sign of his confidence.’
mn125:11.2: ‘But, venerable sir, how could these two similes—never heard before—occur to me in regard to Prince Jayasena, without wonder, as they occur to the Blessed One?’
mn125:12.1: ‘Suppose, Aggivessana, a head-anointed warrior-noble king addressed his elephant woodsman thus:
mn125:12.2: “Come, good elephant woodsman, mount the king’s elephant, enter the elephant wood, and having seen a forest elephant, fasten him by the neck to the king’s elephant.”
mn125:12.3: ‘Yes, sire,’ the elephant woodsman replied to the head-anointed warrior-noble king, and, mounting the king’s elephant, he entered the elephant wood, and having seen a forest elephant, he fastened him by the neck to the king’s elephant.
mn125:12.4: Then the king’s elephant led him out into the open.
mn125:12.5: And that is how, Aggivessana, the forest elephant comes into the open;
mn125:12.6: for forest elephants, Aggivessana, cleave to that, that is to say, the elephant wood.
mn125:12.7: Then the elephant woodsman reported to the head-anointed warrior-noble king:
mn125:12.8: “Sire, the forest elephant has come into the open.”
mn125:12.9: Then, Aggivessana, the head-anointed warrior-noble king addressed the elephant-tamer thus:
mn125:12.10: “Come, good elephant-tamer, tame the forest elephant, in order to subdue his forest habits, in order to subdue his forest memories and intentions, in order to subdue his forest distress, fatigue, and fever, in order to get him to delight in the town, and in order to accustom him to habits pleasing to men.”
mn125:12.11: ‘Yes, sire,’ the elephant-tamer replied to the head-anointed warrior-noble king; and he embedded a large post in the earth and fastened the forest elephant to it by the neck, in order to subdue his forest habits, in order to subdue his forest memories and intentions, in order to subdue his forest distress, fatigue, and fever, in order to get him to delight in the town, and in order to accustom him to habits pleasing to men.
mn125:12.12: Then the elephant-tamer treats him with such words as are innocent, pleasing to the ear, and lovable, as go to the heart, are civil, desired of many, and dear to many.
mn125:12.13: Since, Aggivessana, the forest elephant, being treated by the elephant-tamer with such words as are innocent, pleasing to the ear, and lovable, as go to the heart, are civil, desired of many, and dear to many, is willing to hear, gives ear, and establishes his mind in knowledge,
mn125:12.14: then the elephant-tamer rewards him further with grass fodder and water.
mn125:12.15: Since, Aggivessana, the forest elephant accepts the grass fodder and water from the elephant-tamer, it occurs to the elephant-tamer thus:
mn125:12.17: Then the elephant-tamer makes him carry out a further exercise:
mn125:12.19: Since, Aggivessana, the forest elephant obeys the elephant-tamer’s order to take up and put down and carries out his instructions, then the elephant-tamer makes him carry out a further exercise:
mn125:12.21: Since, Aggivessana, the forest elephant obeys the elephant-tamer’s order to go forward and go back and carries out his instructions, then the elephant-tamer makes him carry out a further exercise:
mn125:12.23: Since, Aggivessana, the forest elephant obeys the elephant-tamer’s order to get up and sit down and carries out his instructions, then the elephant-tamer makes him carry out a further exercise called imperturbability: he fastens a great shield to his trunk, a man with a lance in his hand sits on his neck, men with lances in their hands stand surrounding him on all sides, and the elephant-tamer himself stands in front of him holding a long lance pole.
mn125:12.24: As he carries out the exercise of imperturbability, he moves neither his fore feet nor his hind feet, neither the fore part nor the hind part of his body, nor his head, nor his ears, nor his tusks, nor his tail, nor his trunk.
mn125:12.25: The forest elephant becomes one who endures blows from spears, swords, arrows, and other weapons, and the sounds of drums, kettledrums, conches, and tabors; and being rid of all faults and defects, with flaws removed, he becomes worthy of the king, in the king’s service, and is reckoned as one of the king’s limbs.
mn125:13.1: ‘So too, Aggivessana, here a Tathāgata appears in the world, Arahant, Fully Enlightened, perfect in true knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, incomparable leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and men, enlightened, blessed.
mn125:13.2: He declares this world with its gods, its Māras, its Brahmās, this generation with its monks and divines, with its princes and men, which he has himself realized by direct knowledge.
mn125:13.3: He teaches the Dhamma good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, and he proclaims the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure.
mn125:14.1: ‘A householder or a householder’s son or one born in some other clan hears that Dhamma.
mn125:14.2: On hearing that Dhamma, he acquires faith in the Tathāgata.
mn125:14.3: Possessing that faith he considers thus:
mn125:14.4: “Household life is crowded and dusty; life gone forth is wide open.
mn125:14.5: It is not easy, living in a household, to lead the holy life as utterly perfect and pure as a polished shell.
mn125:14.6: Suppose I shaved off my hair and beard, put on the yellow robe, and went forth from the home life into homelessness?”
mn125:14.7: On a later occasion, abandoning a small or a large fortune, abandoning a small or a large circle of relatives, he shaves off his hair and beard, puts on the yellow robe, and goes forth from the home life into homelessness.
mn125:14.8: That is how, Aggivessana, a disciple of the Noble Ones comes into the open;
mn125:14.9: for gods and men, Aggivessana, cleave to that, that is to say, the five cords of sensual desire.
mn125:15.2: “Come, bhikkhu, be virtuous, restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, and, seeing danger in the slightest fault, train by undertaking the training precepts.”
mn125:16.1: ‘When, Aggivessana, the bhikkhu is virtuous, restrained with the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, and, seeing danger in the slightest fault, trains by undertaking the training precepts, the Tathāgata disciplines him further:
mn125:16.2: “Come, bhikkhu, guard the doors of the faculties. On seeing a form with the eye, do not grasp at its signs and features. Since, if you left the eye faculty unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade you, practise the way of its restraint, guard the eye faculty, undertake the restraint of the eye faculty. On hearing a sound with the ear …
mn125:17-21.1:
on smelling an odour with the nose … on tasting a flavour with the tongue … on touching a tangible with the body … on cognizing a dhamma with the mind, do not grasp at its signs and features. Since, if you left the mind faculty unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade you, practise the way of its restraint, guard the mind faculty, undertake the restraint of the mind faculty.”

‘When, Aggivessana, the bhikkhu guards the doors of the faculties, the Tathāgata disciplines him further: “Come, bhikkhu, be one who knows the right amount in eating. Reflecting wisely, you should take food neither for amusement nor for intoxication nor for smartening nor for embellishment, but only for the endurance and continuance of this body, for ending discomfort, and for assisting the holy life, thinking: ‘Thus I shall terminate old feelings without arousing new feelings, and I shall be healthy and blameless and live in comfort.’”

‘When, Aggivessana, the bhikkhu knows the right amount in eating, the Tathāgata disciplines him further: “Come, bhikkhu, abide devoted to wakefulness. By day, while walking back and forth and sitting, purify your mind of obstructive dhammas. In the first watch of the night, while walking back and forth and sitting, purify your mind of obstructive dhammas. In the middle watch of the night, lie down on the right side in the lion’s pose, with one foot overlapping the other, mindful and fully aware, having noted in your mind the time for rising. After rising, in the third watch of the night, while walking back and forth and sitting, purify your mind of obstructive dhammas.”

‘When, Aggivessana, the bhikkhu is devoted to wakefulness, the Tathāgata disciplines him further: “Come, bhikkhu, possess mindfulness and full awareness. Act in full awareness when going forward and returning; act in full awareness when looking ahead and looking away; act in full awareness when flexing and extending your limbs; act in full awareness when wearing your outer cloak, bowl and robes; act in full awareness when eating, drinking, chewing and tasting; act in full awareness when defecating and urinating; act in full awareness when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, talking and keeping silent.”

‘When, Aggivessana, the bhikkhu possesses mindfulness and full awareness, the Tathāgata disciplines him further: “Come, bhikkhu, resort to a secluded resting place—the forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, a heap of straw.”

He resorts to a secluded resting place—the forest, the root of a tree, a mountain, a ravine, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, a heap of straw. On returning from his alms round, after his meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him. Abandoning covetousness for the world, he abides with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness. Abandoning ill-will and hatred, he abides with a mind free from ill-will, compassionate for the welfare of all living beings; he purifies his mind of ill-will and hatred. Abandoning lethargy and drowsiness, he abides free from lethargy and drowsiness, percipient of light, mindful and fully aware; he purifies his mind of lethargy and drowsiness. Abandoning agitation and worry, he abides unagitated with a mind stilled within; he purifies his mind of agitation and worry. Abandoning uncertainty, he abides having crossed beyond uncertainty, unperplexed about profitable dhammas; he purifies his mind of uncertainty.
mn125:22.1: ‘Having abandoned these five hindrances, imperfections of mind that weaken understanding,
mn125:22.2: he abides contemplating the body as a body, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.
mn125:23.1: He abides contemplating feelings as feelings …
mn125:23.3: he abides contemplating dhammas as dhammas, ardent, fully aware, and mindful, having put away covetousness and grief for the world.
mn125:23.4: Just as, Aggivessana, the elephant-tamer embeds a large post in the earth and fastens the forest elephant to it by the neck, in order to subdue his forest habits, in order to subdue his forest memories and intentions, in order to subdue his forest distress, fatigue, and fever, in order to get him to delight in the town, and in order to accustom him to habits pleasing to men;
mn125:23.5: so too, Aggivessana, these four foundations of mindfulness are the fastening for the mind of a disciple of the Noble Ones, in order to subdue his house-based habits, in order to subdue his house-based memories and intentions, in order to subdue his house-based distress, fatigue, and fever, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of Nibbāna.
mn125:24.2: “Come, bhikkhu, abide contemplating the body as a body, but do not think thoughts connected with the body.
mn125:24.5: abide contemplating dhammas as dhammas, but do not think thoughts connected with dhammas.”
mn125:25.1: ‘With the stilling of initial and sustained application, he enters upon and abides in the second jhāna …
mn125:25.3: he enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna.
mn125:26.1: ‘When his concentrated mind is thus purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs, he inclines the mind to knowledge of the recollection of past life.
mn125:26.2: He recollects his manifold past life, that is to say, one birth, two births …he recollects his manifold past life with its details and particulars.
mn125:27-28.1: ‘When his concentrated mind is thus purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs, he inclines the mind to knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings.
mn125:27-28.2: With the heavenly eyesight, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing, inferior and superior, fair and ugly, well-behaved and ill-behaved … he understands how beings pass on according to their kamma.
mn125:29.1: ‘When his concentrated mind is thus purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs, he inclines the mind to knowledge of the exhaustion of taints.
mn125:29.2: He has direct knowledge thus: “This is suffering”; he has direct knowledge thus: “This is the origin of suffering”; he has direct knowledge thus: “This is the cessation of suffering”; he has direct knowledge thus: “This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering”.
mn125:29.3: He has direct knowledge thus: “These are taints”; he has direct knowledge thus: “This is the origin of taints”; he has direct knowledge thus: “This is the cessation of taints”; he has direct knowledge thus: “This is the way leading to the cessation of taints”.
mn125:29.4: When he knows and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the taint of being, the mind is liberated from the taint of ignorance.
mn125:29.5: When liberated, there comes the knowledge: “It is liberated.”
mn125:29.6: He understands: “Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived out, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.”
mn125:30.1: ‘That bhikkhu becomes one who bears cold and heat, hunger and thirst, and contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things, who endures ill-spoken, unwelcome words, and who is of a nature to bear arisen bodily feelings that are painful, racking, sharp, piercing, disagreeable, distressing, and menacing to life;
mn125:30.2: being rid of all lust, hatred, and delusion, with flaws removed, he becomes fit for gifts, fit for hospitality, fit for offerings, fit for reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
mn125:31.1: ‘If, Aggivessana, an old king’s elephant, untamed and undisciplined, dies, it is reckoned as “an untamed old king’s elephant that has died an untamed death”;
mn125:31.2: if a middle-aged king’s elephant, Aggivessana …
mn125:31.3: if a young king’s elephant, Aggivessana, untamed and undisciplined, dies, it is reckoned as “an untamed young king’s elephant that has died an untamed death”;
mn125:31.4: so too, Aggivessana, if an elder bhikkhu with taints unexhausted dies, it is reckoned as “an elder bhikkhu who has died an untamed death”;
mn125:31.6: if a new bhikkhu, Aggivessana, with taints unexhausted dies, it is reckoned as “a new bhikkhu who has died an untamed death”.
mn125:32.1: ‘If, Aggivessana, an old king’s elephant, well-tamed and well-disciplined, dies, it is reckoned as “a tamed old king’s elephant that has died a tamed death”;
mn125:32.2: if a middle-aged king’s elephant, Aggivessana …
mn125:32.3: if a young king’s elephant, Aggivessana, well-tamed and well-disciplined, dies, it is reckoned as “a tamed young king’s elephant that has died a tamed death”;
mn125:32.4: so too, Aggivessana, if an elder bhikkhu with taints exhausted dies, it is reckoned as “an elder bhikkhu who has died a tamed death”;
mn125:32.6: if a new bhikkhu, Aggivessana, with taints exhausted dies, it is reckoned as “a new bhikkhu who has died a tamed death”.’
mn125:32.7: This is what the Blessed One said.
mn125:32.8: The novice Aciravata was satisfied and delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
